title: Teaching the Cab saxophone section; playing solos for absent soloists
summary: Brown and Hilton Jefferson study with Merle; Thomas takes a back seat to Chu Berry and Ben Webster and can still cover for absent soloists such as Illinois Jacquet.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Now, here's another thing I did, that happened. After I studied, Andrew Brown, he studied. And then when Jefferson come in the band, Jefferson studied. And I'll tell you just one thing about Hilton Jefferson. He got that system faster than anybody I've ever seen. Because Jefferson was a good... He was a good saxophone player, but he had a small tone; he didn't have no big tone. But see, Merle, the way Merle taught you to play, you had a big sound. And I'll tell anybody this. Nobody had a saxophone section like we had. Nobody.
[INAUDIBLE NAME] talks about studying with Merle Johnson.

Yeah. Because he studied with Merle at the same time I did. And all the guys liked me, because see, I was one of the first Black guys to go up there and study. So I was like a... And I was playing with Cab, too.

And I remember one thing that Merle told me. See, I was the first guy to play the solos. So when Chu came in, I knew Chu could play better than me, so Chu started playing the solos. And you know when Ben Webster comes in, I had to take...

Yeah. I had to take a back seat to Ben. And it disturbed me a little bit, because I wasn't playing no more solos. The only solos I got a chance to play was the sweet solos, which I made the arrangements. So I went back and told Merle. He said, "Well, man, don't worry about that." He said, "You've been playing them solos all these years. And remember, every time another guy is playing a solo, you're resting." It made sense. So I just started enjoying hearing Ben and anybody else play.

And another thing they couldn't understand. If any of the saxophone players that was playing their solos was out for some reason or another, I could play the solos. Because I remember one time that Illinois Jacquet was in the band, and he got sick or something and he was out for two or three days. We was playing in one of them big clubs over there in Jersey. And when his solo come up, I just played his solo. Because I'd sat down and listened to the chord structure. All I needed to know was the chord structure. And when the solo came, I could play something. I might not be playing as many notes as them guys, but I was keeping in the chords and making some kind of sound.
And the guys used to wonder how in the heck I did it. But it was from that experience I got out in North
